native_result.query: In which domain do the majority of authors tend to be male for both original and replication studies?
native_result.HypoA: In Experimental Economics, the majority of authors tend to be male for both original and replication studies with ratio of males in original and replication studies being and 0.87 and 0.84 respectively.
native_result.HypoB: Authors tend to be majority male in both the original and the replication study in the ECONOMICS domain (experimental economics, project `ee`). Economics/ee is the only domain majority-male on both sides: mean male-author ratio 0.870 (originals) and 0.837 (replications), author-weighted 0.875/0.814, versus Social 0.658/0.495 and Cognitive 0.711/0.521. 77.8% of Economics originals and 72.2% of its replications are individually majority-male, and 55.6% (10/18) of Economics studies are majority-male in BOTH, versus 36.7% Cognitive, 27.0% Social and 22.7% rpp; no Economics study is majority-female on both sides. The gap is significant against the pooled psychology projects (38/123 = 30.9%; Fisher one-sided p = 0.039, OR = 2.80), though n = 18 gives a wide exact 95% CI on the joint share [30.8%, 78.5%]. The result is stable across every specification (>=0.5, ties excluded, zeros excluded, drop==True excluded, 927-row lab-level view), while the nominal project-level runner-up ml1 leads only through a degenerate pooled consortium replication constant (one value, 0.56, for all 16 studies) and drops to 33.0% using real per-lab replication teams. Caveat: authors_male.* is a binary male/female name-imputed ratio, so non-binary authors are not represented.
native_result.WorkflowB: Read-only inspection of both staged CSVs established that only File A contains authors_male.o/.r (927 rows, 57 cols) and that File B has no gender columns and matches File A on 0/143 keys, so File B was excluded by agreement. Primary unit built as one row per unique `id` (n=141): original-level fields taken once per id (verified constant within id), and for ml1/ml3 the replication male ratio and replication author count taken from the pooled aggregated=True consortium row (verified present for all 26 ml1/ml3 ids); rpp/ee replication ratios taken from their own single row (verified constant within id). Majority male defined as ratio strictly > 0.5, with exactly-0.5 ties tabulated separately. For each discipline (headline) and project (secondary) group computed: n studies, mean authors_male.o and .r, author-count-weighted pooled ratios sum(ratio*n)/sum(n), share of studies majority-male in original, share in replication, and the headline joint share majority-male in both. Seven variants were run: primary; threshold >=0.5; ties excluded; ratio==0 excluded; drop==True excluded; and the 927-row lab-level view, which is reported only as a labelled robustness check because it duplicates each ml1/ml3 original across ~37/~22 labs and therefore over-weights those originals. Economics/ee received an exact Clopper-Pearson interval on the joint share plus a one-sided Fisher exact test against pooled psychology projects. An additional diagnostic found ml1 and ml3 each have a single distinct pooled replication male ratio (0.56, 0.515625) shared by all their studies, so their 100% replication-majority share is degenerate; substituting the real per-lab replication teams moves their joint shares to 33.0% and 34.3%, below ee's 55.6%. Decision rule applied: name the domain leading on the joint per-study share with both mean ratios above 0.5.
